lesson.title: Taxed Enough Already: The Tea Party and the Politics of Backlash
lesson.summary: The Tea Party movement erupted in 2009 as a grassroots protest against federal spending and bailouts, reviving Reagan era small government ideas and reshaping the Republican Party.
lesson.body:
The Tea Party movement emerged in early 2009 as a wave of grassroots protest against federal spending, bank and auto industry bailouts, and the size of government under the new Obama administration. Its name deliberately invoked the Boston Tea Party of 1773, when colonists protested taxation without representation, and its central message was that the federal government was spending, taxing, and regulating too much.

The immediate spark is often traced to February 19, 2009, when CNBC business commentator Rick Santelli, broadcasting live from the floor of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, criticized a federal mortgage relief plan and called for a Chicago tea party to protest it. His remarks spread quickly online and on cable news, and within weeks local protests were forming across the country. These early demonstrations focused on the Troubled Asset Relief Program, the bank bailout signed by President George W. Bush in October 2008, and on the roughly 800 billion dollar American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the economic stimulus package President Obama signed in February 2009. As the year went on, opposition to the Affordable Care Act, the health insurance overhaul Obama signed in March 2010, became a major focus of Tea Party energy as well.

The movement did not have a single national leader or headquarters. It was a mix of local volunteer groups and national organizations, including FreedomWorks and Americans for Prosperity, the latter backed in part by the Koch brothers' network of donors, which provided organizing support, training, and funding. Ideologically, the Tea Party drew heavily on the small government, low tax philosophy associated with the Reagan Revolution of the 1980s, when President Ronald Reagan had argued that government was often the problem rather than the solution and pushed through significant tax cuts. Tea Party activists saw themselves as reviving that tradition after what they viewed as a period of expanding government under Obama.

The movement had significant electoral consequences. In the November 2010 midterm elections, Republicans, boosted by Tea Party energy and candidates, gained 63 seats in the House of Representatives, the largest shift in decades, and took control of the chamber. Many Tea Party aligned candidates also won primary challenges against more moderate Republican incumbents, pulling the party's center of gravity to the right on fiscal issues. Over the following decade, the movement's organizational energy and its emphasis on outsider, anti establishment politics fed into later currents in American conservatism, including the coalition that would support Donald Trump's presidential campaigns. Critics of the movement argued that some of its rhetoric was overheated or that concerns about government spending were applied selectively, while supporters saw it as a genuine citizen response to a period of extraordinary federal intervention in the economy. Both the scale of the 2008 financial crisis and the size of the government response it provoked are well documented, even where interpretations of the Tea Party's motives differ.
